query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thermal-sprayed, corrosion‐resistant coating specifically engineered for high-temperature liquid aluminum environments will form a dense, inert interfacial layer that significantly reduces the rate of erosion and corrosion on components such as rollers and guide plates in hot dip aluminum plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional metal components used in hot dip aluminum plating rapidly erode when exposed to high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a thermal-sprayed protective coating (via plasma or related thermal spraying techniques) on the component surfaces.
generation.conditions: Components are subjected to prolonged exposure in a hot dip aluminum plating process with high-temperature (liquid) aluminum.
generation.structural_mediator: The coating forms a dense and chemically inert interface layer (potentially including refractory or high-entropy alloy phases) that limits interfacial reactions with liquid aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The engineered coating acts as a physical and chemical barrier, reducing direct contact and corrosive reactions between the substrate and liquid aluminum, thereby lowering erosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated components will exhibit a significantly lower material degradation rate and prolonged service life compared to uncoated components under equivalent high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Uncoated components currently experience rapid corrosion and erosion when in direct contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.boundary: The performance of the protective coating may vary with coating composition, thickness, and the thermal cycling or thermal expansion mismatch between the coating and substrate, potentially limiting its effectiveness under extreme or fluctuating conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the overall trend toward improved resistance is supported by surface engineering approaches, the precise magnitude of service life extension and the long-term stability of the coating under dynamic thermal-mechanical stresses remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical roller or guide plate prototypes: one set with the thermal-sprayed protective coating and one set uncoated. Expose both sets to a controlled high-temperature liquid aluminum environment simulating the hot dip plating process. Monitor the components over an extended period to evaluate the rate of material loss and structural degradation.
measurements: Surface morphology and chemical composition analysis via SEM/EDS
Service life estimation via corrosion/erosion rate comparison
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated components do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in material loss (e.g., less than a predetermined threshold reduction in corrosion/erosion rates compared to uncoated controls) under identical conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. “Superalloy” is the general name given to iron-based, nickel-based, and cobalt-based alloys, given their high endurance, creep, and fatigue strength at high temperature. They are widely used in aviation, aerospace, and automotive and chemical industries, serving in high-temperature (≤ 1100 °C) environments. However, for super high temperature conditions of up to 1500 °C and 3000 °C, traditional surperalloys are powerless. Instead, a new type of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown their advantages. High-entropy alloys or multi-element alloys are loosely defined as solid-solution alloys that contain more than five principal elements in equal or near equal atomic percent (at%) [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. HEAs usually have unexpected properties, such as high strength, high hardness, excellent softening resistance, and wear and corrosion resistance [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. According to the cocktail effects of HEAs, the alloy properties can be adjusted by composition changes and via alloying [ [4] , [5] , [10] ]. decision.trend: Over the past years, research in high‐temperature structural and corrosive environments has shifted from modifying bulk compositions and microstructures toward targeted surface and interface engineering. Early work primarily dealt with tailoring alloy compositions and employing post‐processing treatments to improve oxidation resistance or wear properties. More recent studies, such as PMC11077685, have successfully introduced specially designed coatings—using processes like pack cementation—to form beneficial interfacial layers that enhance high‐temperature stability and reduce oxidation. However, none of the previous work has directly resolved the issue of prolonged erosion/corrosion by high-temperature liquid aluminum.
decision.unsolved: A material or coating system that can reliably protect components (rollers, guide plates) in hot dip aluminum plating equipment from the chemically aggressive attack of high-temperature liquid aluminum remains elusive.
decision.lever: thermal spraying for corrosion‐resistant coating design
decision.why: Based on the evolving trend from bulk alloy improvements toward surface modifications, the most plausible next step is to apply a protective coating via thermal spraying (e.g., plasma spraying) that is engineered to resist liquid aluminum attack. This method leverages surface composition modification to form a resilient interface that prevents erosion, directly addressing the performance limitation identified in the niche analysis.
